title: Anatomy of a good prompt
hook: Most weak AI answers start with a weak question. Here is what a good one contains.
points: Swipe for each part and a worked example.
ask: Which of the five do you usually leave out?

slides.title: Role: who the AI should act as
slides.body: For example: 'You are a careful editor.' It sets the tone and the level.

slides.title: Task: what you want done, in one sentence
slides.body: One clear verb: summarise, compare, draft, list, check.

slides.title: Context: what it needs to know
slides.body: Audience, purpose, background. Do not paste customer or company data into an AI tool.

slides.title: Format: how the answer should look
slides.body: A table, five bullets, under 100 words, plain English.

slides.title: Limits: what to avoid
slides.body: Say what to leave out, and ask it to write 'not stated' instead of guessing.

slides.title: A worked example
slides.code: You are a careful editor. Summarise the text below for a busy manager. Use five bullets, under 100 words, plain English. If something is not stated, write 'not stated'. Text: [paste text]

source_note: Written for AI Daily Brief. No claims about any product.

title: How a language model writes an answer
hook: Where does an AI answer actually come from? Five steps, none of them a lookup.
points: It predicts text one piece at a time.
ask: Did you know it works one token at a time?

slides.title: From your question to its answer
flow: Your text is split into tokens
The model scores which token is likely to come next
One token is chosen and added to the text
The steps repeat until the answer is finished
The tokens are turned back into words

slides.title: Likely is not the same as true
slides.body: The model produces probable text. That is why a fluent answer can still be wrong, and why important facts need checking.

source: Google Machine Learning glossary and Wikipedia: Large language model

title: Before you paste: a traffic-light guide
hook: Before you paste anything into an AI tool, ask which colour it is.
points: Your organisation's policy always comes first.
ask: Does your workplace have a rule like this?

slides.title: Public information
slides.body: Something you could say in a public room: a published article, a press release, your own general question.

slides.title: Internal work information
slides.body: Check your organisation's policy before you paste it, and remove names and figures you do not need.

slides.title: Never paste
slides.body: Customer or personal data, passwords, anything confidential. Do not paste customer or company data into an AI tool.

title: Three kinds of machine learning
hook: Three ways a machine learns, each with an everyday picture.
points: Answer key, no answer key, or trial and reward.
ask: Which kind have you seen in a product you use?

slides.title: Learning with an answer key
slides.body: The data comes with the right answers, such as emails already marked spam or not spam.

slides.title: Finding patterns without answers
slides.body: No labels are given. The system looks for groups, such as photos that look alike.

slides.title: Learning by trial and reward
slides.body: The system tries actions and is rewarded for good outcomes, such as a higher score in a game.

items: Usually cheaper and faster to run
Can sometimes run on a laptop
May be weaker on hard tasks
Can be trained to imitate a larger one (distillation)

items: Often more capable on hard tasks
Costs more and is slower
Usually needs cloud hardware
Not always necessary for simple work

title: Open weights or open source?
hook: 'Open' means different things for AI models.
points: Two phrases that are often mixed up.
ask: Do you check a model's licence before using it?

left.head: Open weights
items: The trained parameters are published
You can usually run the model yourself
The training data and code may not be shared
The licence may limit how you use it

right.head: Open source
items: The licence lets you use, study, change and share it
Usually implies more than the weights
Check which licence it really is
Definitions for AI are still debated

slides.title: Read the licence
slides.body: Do not assume. The words on the label matter less than the licence text.

Low risk of side effects

title: Quiz: spot the false statement
hook: One of these three statements is wrong. Which?
points: Three statements about how AI works.
ask: Which one did you pick?

slides.title: Which one is wrong?
options: The transformer design was introduced in 2017 in the paper 'Attention Is All You Need'.
Retrieval-augmented generation requires retraining the whole model on your documents.
Prompt injection is listed by OWASP among the main security risks for applications built on language models.

slides.title: B is wrong
slides.body: RAG looks documents up when you ask, so it does not need the model to be retrained.

slides.title: Check the confident ones
slides.body: Wrong statements often sound as sure as right ones. Check a source.
